claim: The C. elegans egg-laying circuit consists of four type 1 vulval muscle cells (vm1) and four type 2 vulval muscle cells (vm2).
source: The C. elegans egg-laying circuit consists four type 1 vulval muscle cells (vm1) and four type 2 vulval muscle cells (vm2), which form two X-shaped structures near the vulval opening (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1A showing the circuit organization.

claim: vm1 and vm2 form two X-shaped structures near the vulval opening.
source: The C. elegans egg-laying circuit consists four type 1 vulval muscle cells (vm1) and four type 2 vulval muscle cells (vm2), which form two X-shaped structures near the vulval opening (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage.
source: While vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage, are physically adjacent and share many molecular components, the egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2 (White et al., 1986; Waggoner et al., 1998; Duerr et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with supporting citations.

claim: The egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2.
source: While vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage, are physically adjacent and share many molecular components, the egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2 (White et al., 1986; Waggoner et al., 1998; Duerr et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated with multiple supporting citations from prior literature.

claim: vm1 is mainly controlled by vm2 via gap junctions.
source: vm1 is mainly controlled by vm2 via gap junctions (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: UNC-103E is dramatically enriched on vm2 muscle arms.
source: While high level of UNC-103E::GFP expression labels both the muscle arms and the vm cell bodies (Figure 1C), low level of transgenic expression of UNC-103E::GFP with an integrated single-copy transgene showed that UNC-103E was dramatically enriched on vm2 muscle arms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, middle), indicating that the muscle arms represent functional postsynaptic specializations (Collins and Koelle, 2012).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing enrichment and citation to Collins and Koelle, 2012.

claim: The muscle arms represent functional postsynaptic specializations.
source: While high level of UNC-103E::GFP expression labels both the muscle arms and the vm cell bodies (Figure 1C), low level of transgenic expression of UNC-103E::GFP with an integrated single-copy transgene showed that UNC-103E was dramatically enriched on vm2 muscle arms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, middle), indicating that the muscle arms represent functional postsynaptic specializations (Collins and Koelle, 2012).
evidence: Inference drawn from UNC-103E enrichment data with supporting citation.

claim: HSN axon guidance and presynaptic formation preceded both axon growth of VC neurons and vulval muscle differentiation.
source: Developmental studies showed that HSN axon guidance and presynaptic formation preceded both axon growth of VC neurons and vulval muscle differentiation (data not shown).
evidence: Stated based on developmental studies, though data not shown in manuscript.

claim: In egl-1(n986) mutants, HSN neurons undergo programmed cell death in embryonic stage.
source: We therefore asked whether the HSN neurons are required for vm2 specification and muscle arm development by examining the vm2 morphology in the egl-1(n986) mutant, in which the HSN neurons undergo programmed cell death in embryonic stage (Conradt and Horvitz, 1998).
evidence: Stated with citation to Conradt and Horvitz, 1998.

claim: In egl-1(n986) mutants, the morphology and position of vm2 muscle arms were indistinguishable from wild type.
source: Surprisingly, in all of the examined animals, the morphology and position of vm2 muscle arms were indistinguishable from the wild type counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing the phenotype.

claim: Presynaptic components are dispensable for vm2 postsynaptic development.
source: These results indicate that presynaptic components are dispensable for vm2 postsynaptic development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing normal vm2 development in absence of HSN and VC neurons.

claim: In lin-3(e1417) mutant animals, vulval epithelial cell fate is abnormal.
source: We examined the vm2 muscle arm morphology in lin-3(e1417) mutant animals, in which vulval epithelial cell fate is abnormal (Hill and Sternberg, 1992), and observed severe defects on both vulval muscle morphology and muscle arm development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated with citation to Hill and Sternberg, 1992.

claim: lin-3(e1417) mutants show severe defects on both vulval muscle morphology and muscle arm development.
source: We examined the vm2 muscle arm morphology in lin-3(e1417) mutant animals, in which vulval epithelial cell fate is abnormal (Hill and Sternberg, 1992), and observed severe defects on both vulval muscle morphology and muscle arm development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Vulval epithelial cells are required for normal vulval muscle differentiation and morphogenesis.
source: This result suggests that the vulval epithelial cells are required for normal vulval muscle differentiation and morphogenesis, and therefore might be also important for vm2 postsynaptic muscle arm development.
evidence: Inference drawn from lin-3 mutant phenotype.

claim: Six individual mutants representing three complementation groups were isolated in which the vm2 muscle arms were largely absent.
source: In total, six individual mutants representing three complementation groups were isolated in which the vm2 muscle arms were largely absent (Figure 1D,E and Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1D,E and Table 1 showing the mutants.

claim: The isolated mutations affected genes in LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway including lin-12/Notch, apx-1/DSL and sel-12/presinilin.
source: Mapping and molecular identification of these mutations showed that they affected genes in LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway including lin-12/Notch, apx-1/DSL and sel-12/presinilin (Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) mutant animals, the SER-1B::GFP labeled vm2 muscle arm structures were completely absent.
source: In lin-12(wy750) mutant animals, while the muscle morphology of both vm1 and vm2 were largely normal, the SER-1B::GFP labeled vm2 muscle arm structures were completely absent (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1D,E showing the phenotype.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) mutants, both HSN and VC presynaptic markers appeared normal.
source: Both HSN and VC presynaptic markers appeared normal in the lin-12(wy750) mutant, indicating that the mutation specifically affected postsynaptic differentiation and development (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D.

claim: lin-12(wy750) mutation specifically affected postsynaptic differentiation and development.
source: Both HSN and VC presynaptic markers appeared normal in the lin-12(wy750) mutant, indicating that the mutation specifically affected postsynaptic differentiation and development (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D).
evidence: Inference drawn from normal presynaptic markers in the mutant.

claim: No vulval morphogenesis defect was found in lin-12(wy750) mutants by differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy or the localization pattern of the ajm-1::gfp apical junction marker.
source: Surprisingly, we found no vulval morphogenesis defect in lin-12(wy750) mutants either by differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy or the localization pattern of the ajm-1::gfp apical junction marker at several development stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and data not shown) (Koppen et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and citation.

claim: Mutants with defective vm2 muscle arm development laid notably fewer eggs compared to wild-type animals.
source: First, the muscle arm defective mutants laid notably fewer eggs compared to the wild-type animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2A showing egg-laying data.

claim: Muscle arm defective mutants laid more late-stage eggs and fewer early-stage eggs compared with wild-type animals.
source: Indeed, we found that these mutants laid more late-stage eggs and fewer early-stage eggs compared with wild-type animals (Figure 2B), indicative of defects in the egg-laying circuit.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2B showing egg stage distribution.

claim: In wild-type animals, simultaneous Ca2+ transients in the anterior and posterior vulval muscles drive synchronous muscle contraction and release of eggs.
source: In wild-type animals, simultaneous Ca2+ transients in the anterior and posterior vulval muscles, which we call 'double' transients, drive synchronous muscle contraction and release of eggs (Collins and Koelle, 2012) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2C and citation to Collins and Koelle, 2012.

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) vm2 muscle arm mutants were still able to execute single anterior and posterior vulval muscle Ca2+ transients.
source: Despite their lack of postsynaptic muscle arms, we found that lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) vm2 muscle arm mutants were still able to execute single anterior and posterior vulval muscle Ca2+ transients, which was presumably due to the intact minor synaptic inputs from the ventral nerve cord alongside the vulval muscles (Collins and Koelle, 2012).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Collins and Koelle, 2012.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants, double Ca2+ transients were often asynchronous, with significant delays between anterior and posterior vulval muscle transients.
source: However, double Ca2+ transients were often asynchronous, with significant delays between anterior and posterior vulval muscle transients that resulted in uncoordinated vulval muscle contractions that were not able to release eggs (Figure 2D and Video 2).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had a twofold increase in the frequency of Ca2+ transient peaks.
source: As a result, lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had a twofold increase in the frequency of Ca2+ transient peaks (Figure 2H).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2H showing quantification.

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had significantly fewer synchronous double transients compared to the wild type.
source: We also found that lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had significantly fewer synchronous double transients compared to the wild type (Figure 2I).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2I showing quantification.

claim: In wild-type animals, the average anterior/posterior delay in double Ca2+ transients was only ∼100 ms.
source: In wild-type animals, the average anterior/posterior delay was only ∼100 ms (Figure 2J), as nearly all double transients were not resolved into separate anterior/posterior peaks at the temporal and spatial resolution of our ΔR/R traces (Figure 2E).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2J showing quantification.

claim: In both lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants, the average anterior/posterior delay in double Ca2+ transients increased to ∼800 ms.
source: In both lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants, the average anterior/posterior delay in double Ca2+ transients increased to ∼800 ms (Figure 2J) and anterior/posterior transients were easily resolved (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2J showing quantification.

claim: The vm2 muscle arms are required for the synchronous excitation of anterior and posterior vulval muscles needed to successfully execute egg-laying behavior.
source: Together, these results show that the vm2 muscle arms lacking in lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants are not necessary for excitation of the vulval muscles, but suggest they are required for the synchronous excitation of anterior and posterior vulval muscles needed to successfully execute egg-laying behavior.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Ca2+ imaging experiments.

claim: lin-12(wy750) contained a single missense mutation (G473R) in one of the conserved extracellular EGF domains of the LIN-12 protein.
source: Sequence analyses revealed that lin-12(wy750) contained a single missense mutation (G473R) in one of the conserved extracellular EGF domains of the LIN-12 protein (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Table 1 showing the mutation.

claim: lin-12(wy750) is a loss-of-function allele.
source: Two additional results indicated that lin-12(wy750) was a loss-of-function allele. First, trans-heterozygotes between lin-12(wy750) and a canonical loss-of-function allele lin-12(n676n930) presented similar muscle arm defects (data not shown). Second, a lin-12 genomic fragment including 5 kb of upstream regulatory sequence and the entire coding region of lin-12 strongly rescued the muscle arm phenotype of lin-12(wy750) mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: Inference from genetic complementation and rescue experiments.

claim: The missense mutation in lin-12(wy750) represents a partial loss-of-function allele.
source: Since strong loss-of-function alleles of lin-12, apx-1 and sel-12 cause lethality, dramatic vulval morphogenesis or general muscle morphology phenotypes, which are all absent in lin-12(wy750) mutant animals, it is likely that the missense mutation we isolated represents a partial loss-of-function allele.
evidence: Inference from comparison with known strong loss-of-function alleles.

claim: Partial loss of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity spares vulval morphogenesis but specifically impairs vm2 specification and muscle arm development.
source: Together, these data suggest that partial loss of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity spares vulval morphogenesis but specifically impairs vm2 specification and muscle arm development, and that muscle arm development might require a higher level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity compared with earlier developmental events (see 'Discussion').
evidence: Conclusion drawn from phenotypic analysis of partial loss-of-function alleles.

claim: Muscle arm development might require a higher level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity compared with earlier developmental events.
source: Together, these data suggest that partial loss of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity spares vulval morphogenesis but specifically impairs vm2 specification and muscle arm development, and that muscle arm development might require a higher level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity compared with earlier developmental events (see 'Discussion').
evidence: Speculation based on differential sensitivity of developmental processes to LIN-12 activity.

claim: lin-12(n676n930) mutant animals grown at the permissive temperature had no egg-laying defect and showed intact vulval muscle morphology and vm2 muscle arms.
source: Consistent with previous behavioral studies, lin-12(n676n930) mutant animals grown at the permissive temperature had no egg-laying defect and showed intact vulval muscle morphology and vm2 muscle arms, whereas animals grown at the restrictive temperature retained significantly more unlaid eggs inside their bodies and displayed vulval morphogenesis and vulval muscle arm defects.
evidence: Directly stated from temperature shift experiments.

claim: Most lin-12(n676n930) animals shifted from 15°C to 25°C prior to mid-L4 stage showed muscle arm defects similar to those of lin-12(wy750).
source: Most of the animals shifted from 15°C to 25°C prior to mid-L4 stage showed muscle arm defects similar to those of lin-12(wy750), whereas the wild-type muscle arm phenotype was observed in most of lin-12(n676n930) animals that were shifted after mid-L4 stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 3A showing temperature shift results.

claim: lin-12 has a novel function at the L4 stage in regulating the postsynaptic muscle arm development and synaptic target choice.
source: The upshift and downshift experiments together suggest a novel function of lin-12 at the L4 stage in regulating the postsynaptic muscle arm development and synaptic target choice. This lin-12 function is independent of other known roles of lin-12, all of which occur prior to early-L4 stage.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from temperature shift experiments.

claim: The L4 stage function of lin-12 is independent of other known roles of lin-12, all of which occur prior to early-L4 stage.
source: The upshift and downshift experiments together suggest a novel function of lin-12 at the L4 stage in regulating the postsynaptic muscle arm development and synaptic target choice. This lin-12 function is independent of other known roles of lin-12, all of which occur prior to early-L4 stage.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from temporal analysis of lin-12 function.

claim: lin-12 is expressed in both the vm2 muscle cells and the vulval epithelial cells.
source: Transgenic animals carrying this construct showed mCherry expression in a number of cell types including both the vm2 muscle cells (outlined by dashed lines in Figure 4A,B) and the vulval epithelial cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4A,B showing expression pattern.

claim: No detectable lin-12 expression was observed in vm1 muscle cells.
source: Strikingly, no detectable lin-12 expression was observed in vm1 muscle cells.
evidence: Directly stated from expression analysis.

claim: lin-12 functions cell-autonomously in vm2 to specify vm2 postsynaptic development through regulating muscle arm formation.
source: The mosaic rescue analyses argue that lin-12 functions cell-autonomously in vm2 to specify vm2 postsynaptic development through regulating muscle arm formation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mosaic rescue experiments.

claim: APX-1/Dsl is a ligand of LIN-12/Notch.
source: APX-1/Dsl is a good candidate as the relevant ligand because apx-1(wy755), but not other known LIN-12 ligand mutants including dsl-1 and lag-2, showed the muscle arm phenotype similar to that of lin-12(wy750) (Figure 1D and data not shown).
evidence: Inference from genetic analysis and known molecular interactions.

claim: apx-1 and lin-12 function in the same pathway.
source: A lin-12(wy750); apx-1(wy755) double mutant did not show an enhanced muscle arm defect (Figure 4D) or more severe egg-laying phenotype (Figure 2A), further suggesting that apx-1 and lin-12 function in the same pathway.
evidence: Inference from double mutant analysis showing no enhancement.

claim: apx-1 is expressed in both secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 muscle cells during the L4 stage.
source: We observed the expression of apx-1 in both secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 muscle cells during the L4 stage, when LIN-12/Notch signaling was activated to promote vm2 muscle arm development (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Cell-specific expression of apx-1 in either secondary vulval epithelial cells or vm1 muscle cells rescued the muscle arm defects of apx-1(wy755) mutants.
source: Cell-specific expression of apx-1 in either secondary vulval epithelial cells or vm1 muscle cells rescued the muscle arm defects of apx-1(wy755) mutants (Figure 4F).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4F showing rescue data.

claim: apx-1 functions in the vm1 and secondary vulval epithelial cells to activate LIN-12/Notch signaling in vm2, the postsynaptic target cells.
source: These data strongly suggest that apx-1 functions in the vm1 and secondary vulval epithelial cells to activate LIN-12/Notch signaling in vm2, the postsynaptic target cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from expression and rescue experiments.

claim: sel-12 encodes the γ-secretase that releases the LIN-12/NOTCH intracellular domain (NICD) by ligand-induced cleavage.
source: sel-12 encodes the γ-secretase that releases the LIN-12/NOTCH intracellular domain (NICD) by ligand-induced cleavage (Levitan and Greenwald, 1995; Ray et al., 1999a, 1999b; Selkoe and Kopan, 2003).
evidence: Stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Expression of sel-12 in vulval muscle cells completely rescued the vm2 muscle arm phenotype of sel-12(wy760).
source: We found that expression of sel-12 in vulval muscle cells completely rescued the vm2 muscle arm phenotype of sel-12(wy760), consistent with the cell-autonomous requirement of LIN-12/Notch signaling in vm2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4F showing rescue data.

claim: Specific expression of a dominant-negative lag-1 construct in the vulval muscles phenocopied the muscle arm defects observed in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants.
source: Additionally, specific expression of a dominant-negative lag-1 construct (Kato et al., 1997) in the vulval muscles phenocopied the muscle arm defects observed in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants (Figure 4F), suggesting that the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway is likely involved by controlling the transcription of downstream genes.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4F and citation to Kato et al., 1997.

claim: The canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway is likely involved by controlling the transcription of downstream genes.
source: Additionally, specific expression of a dominant-negative lag-1 construct (Kato et al., 1997) in the vulval muscles phenocopied the muscle arm defects observed in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants (Figure 4F), suggesting that the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway is likely involved by controlling the transcription of downstream genes.
evidence: Inference from dominant-negative lag-1 phenotype.

claim: The expression of hlh-29 was dramatically down-regulated in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy755) and sel-12(wy760) mutants.
source: Moreover, the expression of a hlh-29 transcription reporter (hlh-29::gfp), a known target gene of the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2, was also dramatically down-regulated in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy755) and sel-12(wy760) mutants (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) (Fischer and Gessler, 2007; McMiller et al., 2007).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and citations.

claim: APX-1 expressed in the secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells activates the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 to promote the formation of the postsynaptic muscle arms.
source: Together, these results strongly support the model that APX-1 expressed in the secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells activates the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 to promote the formation of the postsynaptic muscle arms.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of genetic and molecular evidence.

claim: The specific activation of the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 but not in vm1 appears to dictate the choice of the synaptic target.
source: The specific activation of the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 but not in vm1 thus appears to dictate the choice of the synaptic target.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from differential LIN-12 activation in vm2 vs vm1.

claim: apx-1(wy755) mutant animals showed significantly reduced expression of lin-12 in vm2 cells.
source: Compared with wild-type animals, apx-1(wy755) mutant animals showed significantly reduced expression of lin-12 in vm2 cells, whereas the lin-12 expression in vulval epithelial cells was not affected (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 5B,C showing expression data.

claim: The apx-1 expression did not change in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: On the other hand, we did not observe any change of apx-1 expression in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 5D).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 5D showing expression data.

claim: apx-1 unilaterally promotes lin-12 expression and activates the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2.
source: These results argue that apx-1 unilaterally promotes lin-12 expression and activates the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from expression analysis in mutants.

claim: Three LAG-1 consensus binding sites were found in the promoter region of lin-12.
source: Indeed, we found three LAG-1 consensus binding sites in the promoter region of lin-12 (Christensen et al., 1996; Maier and Gessler, 2000).
evidence: Stated with citations to Christensen et al., 1996 and Maier and Gessler, 2000.

claim: lin-12(e2621) has a 541-bp deletion in the promoter region leading to the deletion of two of the three LAG-1 binding sites.
source: We sequenced the lin-12 promoter in this allele and found a 541-bp deletion in the promoter region leading to the deletion of two of the three LAG-1 binding sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, top).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing the deletion.

claim: The muscle arm development was similarly affected in lin-12(e2621).
source: Interestingly, the muscle arm development was similarly affected in lin-12(e2621) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, bottom), suggesting that the muscle arm development might require the positive transcriptional feedback of the LIN-12/Notch pathway.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing the phenotype.

claim: The muscle arm development might require the positive transcriptional feedback of the LIN-12/Notch pathway.
source: Interestingly, the muscle arm development was similarly affected in lin-12(e2621) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, bottom), suggesting that the muscle arm development might require the positive transcriptional feedback of the LIN-12/Notch pathway.
evidence: Speculation based on lin-12(e2621) phenotype and promoter deletion.

claim: UNC-40 is a homolog of Deleted in Colorectal Carcinoma (DCC) and neogenin in vertebrates serving as a receptor for the UNC-6/Netrin ligand.
source: UNC-40, which is a homolog of Deleted in Colorectal Carcinoma (DCC) and neogenin in vertebrates serving as a receptor for the UNC-6/Netrin ligand (Serafini et al., 1994; Chan et al., 1996; Keino-Masu et al., 1996), was reported to play a role in muscle arm formation in the body wall muscles (Dixon and Roy, 2005; Alexander et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: UNC-40 was reported to play a role in muscle arm formation in the body wall muscles.
source: UNC-40, which is a homolog of Deleted in Colorectal Carcinoma (DCC) and neogenin in vertebrates serving as a receptor for the UNC-6/Netrin ligand (Serafini et al., 1994; Chan et al., 1996; Keino-Masu et al., 1996), was reported to play a role in muscle arm formation in the body wall muscles (Dixon and Roy, 2005; Alexander et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated with citations to Dixon and Roy, 2005 and Alexander et al., 2009.

claim: MADD-2 directly binds and functions together with UNC-40 to regulate body wall muscle arm extension as well as axon branching and patterning.
source: More recently, MADD-2, a C1-TRIM protein encoding a homolog of human MID1, was shown to directly bind and function together with UNC-40 to regulate body wall muscle arm extension as well as axon branching and patterning (Alexander et al., 2010; Hao et al., 2010; Morikawa et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citations to Alexander et al., 2010, Hao et al., 2010, and Morikawa et al., 2011.

claim: Both unc-40(n324) and madd-2(ok2226) null mutants showed specific vulval muscle arm defects with largely normal vulval muscle morphology.
source: Interestingly, both unc-40(n324) and madd-2(ok2226) null mutants showed specific vulval muscle arm defects with largely normal vulval muscle morphology (Figure 6A and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6A and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: A significant proportion of unc-40 and madd-2 mutant animals completely lacked the vm2 muscle arms.
source: A significant proportion of the mutant animals completely lacked the vm2 muscle arms, while some other animals showed abnormal muscle arms that extended from incorrect positions or flimsy muscle arms that were thinner and dimmer than the wild-type muscle arms (Figure 6B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6B showing quantification.

claim: The muscle arm defects in unc-40 and madd-2 mutants were strongly rescued by expressing unc-40 or madd-2 specifically in vulval muscles.
source: These defects were strongly rescued by expressing unc-40 or madd-2 specifically in vulval muscles in respective mutants, suggesting that both unc-40 and madd-2 function cell-autonomously in vm2 to promote and guide muscle arm growth (Figure 6B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6B showing rescue data.

claim: Both unc-40 and madd-2 function cell-autonomously in vm2 to promote and guide muscle arm growth.
source: These defects were strongly rescued by expressing unc-40 or madd-2 specifically in vulval muscles in respective mutants, suggesting that both unc-40 and madd-2 function cell-autonomously in vm2 to promote and guide muscle arm growth (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inference from cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: The expression of both unc-40 and madd-2 could be robustly detected in the vm2 cells but not in vm1 cells.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that the expression of both unc-40 and madd-2 could be robustly detected in the vm2 cells but not in vm1 cells (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6C,D showing expression patterns.

claim: UNC-40::GFP is enriched on the muscle arms.
source: Moreover, UNC-40::GFP is enriched on the muscle arms, further suggesting that it might function locally to promote muscle arm growth (Figure 6C).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6C showing localization.

claim: The levels of UNC-40 and MADD-2 critically determine the capacity of vulval muscles to grow muscle arms and be selected as the postsynaptic target by the egg-laying motoneurons.
source: These results indicate that the levels of UNC-40 and MADD-2 critically determine the capacity of vulval muscles to grow muscle arms and be selected as the postsynaptic target by the egg-laying motoneurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from expression and mutant analysis.

claim: The expression of both UNC-40 and MADD-2 in vm2 was significantly down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: The expression of both UNC-40 and MADD-2 in vm2 was significantly down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 6C,D), supporting the idea that lin-12 was required for the expression of unc-40 and madd-2 in vm2.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6C,D showing expression in mutant.

claim: lin-12 is required for the expression of unc-40 and madd-2 in vm2.
source: The expression of both UNC-40 and MADD-2 in vm2 was significantly down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 6C,D), supporting the idea that lin-12 was required for the expression of unc-40 and madd-2 in vm2.
evidence: Inference from expression analysis in lin-12 mutant.

claim: Both unc-40 and madd-2 were preferentially transcribed in vm2 cells.
source: Similar transcription pattern was observed for unc-40 and madd-2. Both unc-40 and madd-2 were preferentially transcribed in vm2 cells, and the transcriptional activities of both promoters were dramatically suppressed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B showing transcription patterns.

claim: The transcriptional activities of both unc-40 and madd-2 promoters were dramatically suppressed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: Similar transcription pattern was observed for unc-40 and madd-2. Both unc-40 and madd-2 were preferentially transcribed in vm2 cells, and the transcriptional activities of both promoters were dramatically suppressed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The canonical LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway acts to promote the transcriptions of both unc-40 and madd-2 directly.
source: These data indicate that the canonical LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway acts to promote the transcriptions of both unc-40 and madd-2 directly.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from transcriptional reporter analysis.

claim: Two LAG-1 consensus binding sites were found on the proximal promoter region of the madd-2 gene.

claim: The expression of unc-40 in the lin-12(wy750) mutant was sufficient to induced muscle arm-like membrane extension in vm2 cells in ∼41% of the animals.

evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 7A showing rescue data.

claim: unc-40 has a deterministic role in promoting postsynaptic muscle arm development.
source: We found that the expression of unc-40, but not madd-2, in the lin-12(wy750) mutant was sufficient to induced muscle arm-like membrane extension in vm2 cells in ∼41% (36 of 88) of the animal (Figure 7A and data not shown), suggestive of a deterministic role of unc-40 in promoting postsynaptic muscle arm development.

claim: Misexpression of UNC-40 was sufficient to induce the dendritic spine-like membrane extensions from vm1 cells.
source: We found that misexpression of UNC-40 was sufficient to induce the dendritic spine-like membrane extensions from vm1 cells (Figure 7B).

claim: The ectopic membrane extension from vm1 always formed from the medial surface of vm1, the identical location as for the normal vm2 muscle arms.
source: Although the ectopic membrane extension from vm1 was usually thinner than the wild-type vm2 muscle arm, the vm1 muscle arms always formed from the medial surface of vm1, the identical location as for the normal vm2 muscle arms, suggesting that UNC-40 responds to specific environmental cues to guide the formation of muscle arms.
evidence: Directly stated from observation of ectopic expression phenotype.

claim: The postsynaptic development and synaptic target selection in the egg-laying circuit are mediated by the LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway.
source: We conclude that the postsynaptic development and synaptic target selection in the egg-laying circuit are mediated by the LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway.

source: The secondary vulval epithelial cells and non-target vm1 cells express APX-1/Dsl, which activates its receptor LIN-12/Notch in the vm2 synaptic target cells.

source: The LIN-12/Notch pathway promotes the expression of UNC-40/DCC and MADD-2, which cooperates with each other to generate postsynaptic muscle arms.
evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claim: Vulval morphogenesis requires a low level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activation, while vm2 postsynaptic specification requires a relatively high level of LIN-12/Notch activity.
source: Together, these data strongly argue that vulval morphogenesis requires a low level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activation, while vm2 postsynaptic specification requires a relatively high level of LIN-12/Notch activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analysis of partial loss-of-function alleles.

claim: The formation of pre- and postsynaptic specializations can occur at different times.
source: First, the formation of pre- and postsynaptic specializations can occur at different times. The HSN presynaptic specializations form at the early L4 stage, significantly before the maturation of the postsynaptic targets. The extension of the postsynaptic muscle arms takes place 5–6 hr later.
evidence: Directly stated from developmental timing observations.

claim: The development of the pre- and postsynaptic specializations appears to be independent of each other.
source: Second, the development of the pre- and postsynaptic specializations appears to be independent of each other. Eliminating the postsynaptic cells does not affect the timing and location of synaptic vesicle accumulation in HSN neurons (Shen and Bargmann, 2003). Similarly, ablation of the presynaptic neurons has no obvious effect on the timing and direction of the muscle arm growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Stated with citation and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Pre- and postsynaptic differentiations are guided by two different but related guidepost cells.
source: Third, pre- and postsynaptic differentiations are guided by two different but related guidepost cells.
evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claim: The primary vulval epithelial cells serve as guidepost cells for the HSN presynaptic development.

evidence: Stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Postsynaptic differentiation is likely guided by the secondary vulval epithelial cells.
source: Interestingly, postsynaptic differentiation is likely guided by the secondary vulval epithelial cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).

claim: The muscle arms appear to grow along the interface between the primary and the secondary vulval epithelial cells through possibly an UNC-40-dependent mechanism.

evidence: Inference from muscle arm positioning and UNC-40 function.

claim: The epithelial cells play organizational roles for the development of the entire vulval organ, coordinating multiple events including vulval muscle migration, axon guidance of HSN, VC axon branching and synapse formation.
